@@120732027 <p> The Rafah terminal that marks the crossing between southern Gaza and Egypt straddles a complicated border . On the Egyptian side , a double arch marks the entry to the terminal buildings themselves , and beyond , Gaza . <p> Television cameras on the Egyptian side caught the moment on Saturday that the crossing , which has been closed since May , was reopened for medical evacuations showing one young girl , whose foot had been amputated , being loaded into an Egyptian ambulance . <p> What can not be underestimated is that any reopening of Rafah , even partial , is a moment of considerable significance . <p> Amid the long years of Israeli blockade that followed Hamas 's takeover of the coastal strip in 2007 , Rafah -- the only crossing out of Gaza that does not border Israel -- has been seen as a safety valve as a potential access to the outside world . <p> If it was never really available to many , at least the possibility existed . <p> For a period earlier in the war , Rafah was the exit point for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ or with the financial wherewithal and connections to pay to be put on an Egyptian list to leave . <p> But since Israeli forces launched an offensive in and around the southern city of Rafah in May last year , the border has been closed even for the most urgent medical evacuation cases , with Egypt closing its side in protest . <p> The director general of the World Health Organization , Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus , summed up the situation starkly last month : " Only 5,383 patients have been evacuated from Gaza with support from WHO since October 2023 , of which only 436 since the Rafah crossing was closed . <p> " Over 12,000 people still need medical evacuation . At this rate , it would take five to 10 years to evacuate all these critically ill patients , including thousands of children . In the meantime , their conditions get worse and some die . " <p> Israel has permitted a number of medical evacuations since May , including 55 patients in December , but it has been a drop in the ocean , an assessment @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Ant ? nio Guterres , last week that 2,500 children were in need of immediate evacuation . <p> If opening the crossing to 50 children and their families is a first step as an agreed part of the Gaza ceasefire deal that envisages further regular evacuations , it has another significance too . <p> Hamas releases three more hostages from Gaza under ceasefire deal with Israel -- video <p> While Israeli society has celebrated the release of hostages , ordinary Palestinians in Gaza in the past week have also begun to see benefits to the ceasefire deal beyond the cessation of fighting and killing . <p> Large numbers of residents from the north of the strip have been permitted to return home to the devastated area having been forcibly displaced by Israel . As well as the opening of Rafah , the first Palestinian detainees arrested in Gaza and held in Israel , numbering 111 , were released home on Saturday . <p> Then there is the opening of Rafah itself , facilitated by an arrangement in which the deployment of EU monitors at the crossing to supervise officials from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ West Bank , have been tasked with processing those leaving Gaza . <p> All of which suggests that -- just maybe -- there may be a hint of a potential dynamic for success emerging in the fragile and complex three-phase deal , which to many seemed set up for inevitable failure and a return to Israel 's offensive . <p> After today the next significant milestone will be marked by the planned beginning of negotiations for phase two of the deal next week , amid evidence that the Trump administration in Washington , despite a highly erratic and contradictory grasp of its Middle East policy , is still insisting that both sides cleave to the agreement and see it through . <p> What is clear today is that another important staging post in the deal has been passed , as well as the first small measure of relief for sick and wounded Palestinians .

@@120822210 <h> The growing power of the Amish vote in US politics <p> Religion has not played a central role in this election campaign . It seems that there are other , more immediate issues -- such as the economy , escalating international crises and Kamala 's " joy " levels -- taking precedence in the minds of voters and candidates alike . <p> However , it could be that the voting habits of certain religious minorities end up being the deciding factor in the presidential race . With both international and national conflicts proving to be particularly divisive and polarising , it 's likely that religious blocs , whether holding firm to tradition or breaking up in favour of a new path , may shape the outcome next week . <p> Muslim frustration with both parties ' perceived lack of compassion toward Gaza ; Jewish concerns over left-wing antisemitism on the fringes of the Democrats ; Catholic support mobilising for Vance : once the results are in , religious voting trends will be well worth exploring to explain the result . <p> But perhaps the most endearing of all religious @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Amish . An ultra-conservative sect of Anabaptist Christians , the Amish are best known for their rejection of modern technology . They are easily identifiable by their plain , traditional clothes and their use of horse-drawn buggies instead of cars . <p> Placing high value on a rural , simple life , they are generally not inclined to get involved in party politics . Gelassenheit , a term denoting acceptance of God 's will , and Ordnung , the set of rules governing Amish life , mean they largely remain passive about the world 's outside goings-on . <p> However , as culture wars drive Americans into increasingly polarised camps , the Amish have found themselves taking sides with an eclectic bunch : wellness aficionados , Gwyneth Paltrow , and Donald Trump . And the reason ? Raw milk . <p> Since the 2010s , influencers have been advocating raw milk for its health benefits , with Paltrow saying she takes it in her morning coffee . Despite its potential to cause life-threatening conditions like sepsis and meningitis , raw milk has garnered fans as far afield as the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to health concerns , the U.S. has an array of legal restrictions surrounding raw milk at both federal and state levels . In 1987 , the Food and Drug Administration ( FDA ) issued a federal ban on interstate sale or distribution of raw milk for human consumption , citing public health risks , and since then , a patchwork of state laws has regulated its sale and distribution . <p> Conservative libertarians have taken issue with these restrictions . Generally suspicious of laws that regulate or restrict food choices , they find the prohibition of this most wholesome of drinks entirely wrong and fully support the hipster 's right to infectious illness . <p> They also support raw milk producers , many of whom are Amish , as raw milk production aligns with Amish agricultural practices and self-sufficiency . When Amish farmer Amos Miller 's farm in Lancaster , Pennsylvania , was raided by police for selling raw milk without a licence , it became a rallying point for MAGA supporters advocating Amish farmers ' rights . " <p> While the Amish typically avoid voting , they can sometimes be motivated to participate , as they were in the 1950s when concerns over public school policies -- particularly mandatory high school attendance -- prompted many to vote . <p> With 90,000 Amish living in Pennsylvania , and an estimated 80 percent chance that whoever wins Pennsylvania will win the presidency , it 's unsurprising that Republicans are eager to court the Amish vote . @@120842814 <h> Scottish independence messaging must catch up with globalisation <p> THE era of untrammelled American globalisation is in its closing phases . <p> This does not mean that the United States , with its sprawling military , is not dominant in the world system . But the strategic calculations around how the superpower situates itself are radically shifting . <p> This is not necessarily a managed process , but a forced one , owing to imperial decline and with it the coming apart of the post-war global order . Of course , the brash approach taken by Donald Trump puts exclamation points after this process . <p> But events today are not reducible to a study of his personal psychology or the populist resentments built up within the domestic political arena . Rather , he and his administration are a reflection of something far more structural : that the United States is now one of several great powers , vying for position , in an emerging multi-polar order . <p> Gone are the days when the supranational institutions of American hegemony were unchallenged . <p> This means that nation-states and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are having to consider their position in a volatile and fluctuating world order . <p> This includes Scotland , and has profound implications for the intellectual reconstruction of the case for Scottish independence in the 21st century . <p> Before we get to the meaning behind of actions of the new Trump regime thus far , some further scene-setting is required . <p> The foreign policy disasters attendant to the challenges now confronting American power also lie at the door of the erstwhile Republican establishment and the Democratic leadership . It can not be understated how deleterious the invasion and occupation of Iraq , and the humiliating withdrawal from Afghanistan have been to the US militarily and geopolitically . <p> The same can be said of its approach to the Middle East more recently , where Joe Biden led the most overt charge against the architecture of international humanitarian law , in partnership with Israel 's actions in Gaza . <p> Closer to home , while the export of manufacturing to low-waged economies in the Global South allowed for multi-national corporations to achieve higher profits , and American consumers lower @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ This includes fewer manufacturing jobs , often in areas where people have become supportive of Trump 's campaigning . The US trade deficit with China , for example , eliminated around 3.7 million American jobs between 2001 and 2018 . <p> What is striking about recent days and weeks is the way in which the United States has ranged itself against its allies . <p> Denmark has had it far tougher than Iran , for example . In an aggressive and confrontational phone call with Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen , Trump demanded that Denmark sell Greenland . <p> Remember , Denmark is a Nato member , which makes an already outlandish initiative seem even more deluded . <p> This while the US sparks a diplomatic crisis with Canada , and as Trump says he prefers to deal with individual European states , rather than the European Union , upon which he plans to launch a tariff war . You might call it a modern version of gunboat diplomacy . Meanwhile , Britain is being buffeted by the crosswinds and is denuded of any real agency as far as Keir @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for Trump , in the hope that he is more gracious with Number 10 than he was to the Danes . <p> But do n't believe the claim that this is all simply a passing , outlandish , phase . What we are seeing is a retrenchment of American power . <p> Rather than firing up for new rounds of war in the Middle East -- though this can never be written off entirely -- Europe and its closest neighbours are to be cannibalised . The idea is to subjugate these powers more comprehensively , rather than manage them as orbital allies . <p> Consider that USAID is being shut down . This is one of the most important components of America 's soft-power operation around the world . <p> It shows that the US is retreating , consolidating , and preparing for future great power conflicts , especially with China . <p> Of course , this also opens up new avenues for the tech oligarchy and others to more directly realise their interests . In this global disengagement , Trump and " Maga " are mascots , who rather @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ crude nationalist exceptionalism . <p> The pace of change is astounding , and it demands a serious response . Nothing can be taken for granted about the architecture of the Western system . That includes the European Union , Nato and the concept of the " special " transatlantic relationship with the US . <p> Within this context , new dimensions begin to contour the discussion around Scottish independence . <p> While it is off the agenda in any practical sense , the renewal of the case and a distinctive Scottish political culture must take into consideration the reality of a brave new world . <p> Simply put , the official case , already threadbare and incoherent , needs almost entirely revamped and reimagined . <p> Turning up to a war with a peashooter , First Minister John Swinney says he plans to use Trump 's " affinity for Scotland " in a bid to avoid the prospect of tariffs being applied on imports to the US . <p> If that was not sycophantic enough , Alba 's Ash Regan wrote a letter to tech overlord Elon Musk urging him @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a new " gigafactory " . <p> None of this represents a theory of meaningful Scottish autonomy or guide to action which fits in the new global landscape . <p> It appears that despite the supposed differences between the SNP leadership and the Alba leadership hopeful , both are content with Scotland being a vassal to more powerful states . <p> New thinking is required , and that means first coming to an appraisal of the geopolitical environment . <p> Within this context , there is the potential for fresh ideas to be reinjected into discussions about the meaning of independence and Scotland 's role on the international scene . <p> That thinking will have to come from outside those elements attached to an outdated view of the world , and from those whose ambition for the country is limited to appeasing American power in its revanchist phase . <p> But there is an opening , perhaps the first in some time , for some dynamic and interesting thinking on the national question . <h> Why are you making commenting on The National only available to subscribers ? @@120878901 <p> Imagine , for a moment , that the Iranian government ann ? ounces it has developed a nuc ? lear bomb and threatens to use it on Israel . The United States reacts with the threat of military intervention , as it did in 1991 and 2003 in Iraq . Iran signals that it will not tolerate a third Gulf war and looks for allies . American forces mass to enter Iran , which orders national mobilisation . Russia , China and North Korea express their support for Iran , and Washington expands its intervention force , bringing in a British contingent . Russia enters the game , raising the stakes in the expectation that the West will back down . A nuclear standoff follows , but with tense and itchy fingers on both sides , as leaders gamble on the risk of not striking first , it all ends in disaster . The Third World War begins with an exchange of nuclear fire , and the rest , as they say , is history . <p> Or picture this : Chinese frustration over the status of Taiwan prompts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pre ? occupied with its own domestic political crisis . Japan anxiously watches the exchange of harsh words between China and Taiwan , wondering whether to intervene . The United Nations condemns Chinese actions , and China repudiates the censure and orders invasion , confident that a quick victory will prevent others from intervening , as Hitler hoped when he invaded Poland in 1939 . The United States now activates contingency plans to save Taiwan , and each side uses tactical nuclear weapons against the other 's armed forces . North Korea and Russia side with China . There is no general nuclear strike , but Russia warns Europe to keep out , dividing American strategy between the two theatres , as it was in the Second World War . The conflict continues to escalate . <p> Now let 's consider a totally different kind of global conflict . The growing division between the democratic West and the arc of authoritarian states across Eurasia has entered a dangerous new chapter . Neither side wants to risk outright war , but there is a possibility that destroying satellite communications will undermine @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Without warning , the West 's satellite communication ? system is attacked and massive damage is done to its commercial and military electronic networks . <p> The Siege of Rhodes in 1522 : In every single culture of the past 5,000 years , war has been accepted practice Credit : CPA Media Pte Ltd / Alamy Stock Photo <p> No one claims to have launched the missiles , but , in the chaos that follows , blame is quickly directed at anti-Western states . Retaliation is difficult to mount with the collapse of communications . Uncertain what to do , military mobilisation is ordered across the Western world , but Russia and China demand that it cease . As in 1914 , the wheels , once set in motion , are hard to stop , and the crisis grows . Welcome to the First Space War . <p> These three scenarios are poss ? ible , though not one of them , I should make clear , is probable . ? Predicting -- more accurately , imagining -- the wars of the future can produce dangerous fantasies that promote anxiety @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ most plausible prognosis will be wrong . The development of nuclear weapons has substantially changed the terms of any future global conflict . There are no doubt contingency plans prepared by armed forces everywhere to meet a range of possibilities that might otherwise be regarded as fanciful in the real world . And while history may help us to think about the shape of a future war , the lessons of history are seldom learnt . <p> Yet the question of how a third world war might erupt haunts us today more than at any time since the end of the last world war . The very act of guessing is proof of our expectation that warfare of some kind remains a fact in a world of multiple insecurities . Conflicts in Ukraine , Gaza , Myanmar and Sudan are a reminder of that ever-present reality . And regular threats from Russia about using nuclear weapons suggest that our fantasies may not be so wide of the mark after all . <p> Perhaps , in attempting to forecast the outbreak of a future war , we should ask another question @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has been a characteristic of almost the whole of recorded history , and warlike violence preceded the establishment of the first states . Why human beings have developed belligerency alongside their capacity for social cooperation remains a fundamental question . <p> It is a puzzle with which the human ? sciences have wrestled for much of the 20th and 21st centuries . For evolutionary biologists and psychologists , warfare was a means for early man to ensure survival , protect kin and cope with ecological crisis . No human biologist now argues that violence is in our genes , but early hominins , organised in small bands of hunter-gatherers or fishers , almost certainly used violence to protect against intruders , secure resources and food , and on occasion to act as predators on neighbouring communities . The resort to violence as one of the elements in the survival kit of early man became psychologically normative , as well as biologically useful . On this reading , bell ? igerence is something deeply embedded in human development . <p> Yet this view is challenged by the other sciences , which @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ settled cultures and political systems , whether tribe , proto-state or state . By 10,000 years ago , there is no doubt that something resembling warfare emerged worldwide , evidenced in the archaeological record of weapons , iconography and fortifications . <p> Warfare was not like modern war , organised in mass armies and supplied by military industries , but took a variety of forms : a deadly raid , a ritual encounter , or a massacre , such as the Nataruk killings , dating to the 9th century BC : the remains of men , women ( one of them pregnant ) and children unearthed from this site near Kenya 's Lake Turkana show the victims were clubbed and stabbed to death . <p> It was evidently not necessary to have a state to engage in violence , as the tribal warfare observed in the past few hundred years has demonstrated , but war did mean the emergence of a warrior elite and a culture in which warfare was valorised and endorsed : the Spartans , the Vikings , the Aztecs . There have been very few cultures in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ central part , in the life of the community . In the historic period of states , from about 5,000 years ago , there are no examples where warfare was not accepted practice . <p> This says little about why wars are waged in the archaic past or the present . Wars are always waged for something , whether it is pleasing the gods by seizing captives to ? execute or sacrifice , or coveting resources , or wars for belief , or extending power over others , or in the search for heightened security , or simply a war of defence against a predator . This mix of motives has remained remarkably constant . <p> The seizure of resources is an obvious motivation for war , an explanation that extends from the ancient Romans as they destroyed enemy cities and grabbed slaves and treasure and exacted tribute , to the Japanese forces in 1942 when they captured the oil and raw mat ? erials of South-east Asia needed for waging further war . Wars for belief also span millennia , from the Muslim conquests of the Middle East and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ age of Christian cru ? sades that followed , to the current jihad campaigns of militant Islam . <p> Security , as Thomas Hobbes famously recognised in his Leviathan of 1651 , is always at risk in an anarchic world where there is no single common power to enforce it . Frontiers are a touchstone of security fears and lack of trust , as the wars in Ukraine and Gaza illustrate today . But the long Chinese frontier with the steppe nomads and the vast frontier of the late Roman empire were also sites of constant encroach ? ments , defensive battles and punitive expeditions . <p> Missiles launched during a ground force drill by the Iranian army , October 2023 Credit : Alamy <p> Pursuit of power is perhaps the most common explanation for war -- particularly popular with political and social scientists . Power Transition Theory , pioneered at the height of the Cold War , sees a constant race between major hegemonic powers as one tries to exceed the power of the other . The race , so it is argued , might end in war as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a rising power seeks to replace it . At one time , the theory was applied to the United States and the Soviet Union , but they never went to war against each other ; now it is applied to possible war between the United States and China , which has become a favourite scenario for those predicting 21st-century conflict . Yet it is a ? theory that works poorly . The two world wars began with a major power picking on a lesser one -- ? Serbia in 1914 , Poland in 1939 -- and then dragging other powers into the maelstrom . That might indeed happen with Taiwan , as it is already happening with Ukraine . <p> Power works best as an explanation when history turns to the individuals who drove themselves to become the great conquerors , men whose raw ambition mobilised ? support from their people for unlimited conquest -- Alexander the Great , Genghis Khan , Napoleon , Hitler . This is hubristic power based on arrogant self-belief and it usually evaporates with the death or defeat of the leader . But so long @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ follow , war is unlimited and destructive on a vast scale . This is the most dangerous and unpredictable explanation for the persistence of warfare and it covers the whole historical record . It is one of the surest indications that war still has a future as well as a long past . <p> The wars of the future draw on a grim heritage . The fact that peace would seem to be the rational option for most humans has never been able to stifle the urge to fight when it seems necessary , or lucrative , or an obligation . And that heritage is the chief reason it is possible to imagine a future war . After the end of the Cold War , there was once a fashion for saying that war was obsolete -- if only that were so , we might now live in a world without weapons and fear . While few would actively seek the Third World War , few envisaged or wanted the other two . The sad reality is that our understanding of why wars occur has so far contributed little to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Why War ? by Richard Overy is published by Pelican at ? 22 . This price spike , reaching record levels not seen in decades , fuelled global inflation above 8% in 2022 , increasing living costs and eroding purchasing power , further exacerbating social unrest in many countries . <p> Politically , the war has deepened divisions among major powers , destabilizing the international system and affecting both the Middle East and Europe . Some regional actors have leveraged the crisis to expand their influence , while others find themselves balancing traditional alliances with new strategic partnerships . In Europe , soaring energy costs have hit industries and small businesses hard , jeopardizing national energy security . Meanwhile , in the Middle East , oil-exporting nations have benefited from rising prices , but the increased cost of goods and services has negatively impacted citizens ' purchasing power . <p> Amid these challenges , the world eagerly anticipates an end to the war , widely attributed to provocations by the previous U.S. administration under President @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ can broker peace in this conflict , which poses a significant threat to international stability . His approach combines pressure and incentives to bring both sides to the negotiating table , aiming to restore regional and global stability . <p> Trump 's vision is reflected in the message of his envoy , Keith Kellogg , who recently urged Russia and Ukraine to make mutual concessions for peace . This blend of incentives and deterrence creates a complex dynamic that could ultimately pave the way for resolution . <p> Trump asserts that Ukraine 's ability to sustain the war hinges on continued Western support , with US aid alone reaching approximately $108bn since 2022 , supplemented by European and allied contributions . He argues that halting these funds and arms could shift Ukraine 's calculations , pushing it toward diplomatic solutions rather than prolonged military engagement . <p> Additionally , Trump seeks to reshape the Western narrative framing Ukraine as a defender of democratic values against Russian expansion . This perspective may weaken European support for the war and encourage all parties to consider peaceful alternatives . He also challenges the feasibility of a strategic defeat of Russia , emphasizing that cooperation with Moscow is essential for global stability . Citing Russia 's historical role in European security , Trump questions the effectiveness of costly confrontational policies that , after nearly three years , have failed to yield decisive results . <p> Trump 's past relationship with Putin , based on dialogue and cooperation on geopolitical matters , informs his approach . He argues that the Biden administration 's escalation -- described by some as a " ring of fire " policy -- has worsened tensions with Russia and its neighbours in both Europe and Asia . Consequently , Trump aims to de-escalate these conflicts and foster diplomatic engagement with Moscow , which could lead to serious negotiations to end the war . <p> Moreover , Trump proposes a 20-year ban on Ukraine 's NATO membership -- an essential concession to Moscow addressing one @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ acknowledges Russian control , potentially incentivizing Russia to negotiate . This pragmatic approach could serve as a catalyst for peace , given the war 's damaging effects on the global economy and supply chains . <p> If Trump succeeds in halting the war , it could mark a fundamental shift in global geopolitics , reducing political and military polarization and steering the world toward cooperative rather than adversarial dynamics . I think we can <p> new <h> The president 's use of hyperbole and falsehood makes him sound crazed but there 's a method here -- and it has worked <p> Thursday February 06 2025 , 9.00pm , The Times <p> Even the most worldly , by now inured to the derangements of Donald Trump 's expansive imagination , probably did n't have these on their list of expectations for the first two weeks of Trump II : pressure on Canada to become the 51st US state ; threats of war with Denmark over the annexation of Greenland ; America taking ownership of the Gaza Strip and shipping two million Palestinians to Arab countries . <p> The candidate who promised an end to America 's " forever wars " , railed against wasteful and damaging foreign entanglements and boasted of a first-term record of no major US deployments to far-flung places , has started his second term sounding like a new Caesar , eyeing up vast swathes of territory ripe for incorporation into an expanding imperium . From neo-isolationist @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ we make it make sense ? I think we can . <p> * <p> The overarching explanation for all Trumpian declarations applies here , of course . We should be familiar with the perils of taking the man literally . It is not just that Trump speaks habitually in hyperbole and falsehood , but that he is in a constant game of escalation with his audience . To keep one step ahead of interlocutors on the other side of the table who think they 've got used to the hyperbole , he needs to keep upping it . The only way to stay ahead of the expectations curve is to make ever more outlandish claims . The most inviting thing you can ever say to Trump is : surely you ca n't do that ? <p> But there are , I think , three particular things behind the president 's latest adventures in foreign policy wonderland . On one level , this is " Trump : The Real Estate Mogul Goes Global " . Constantly on the lookout for the most spectacular property development projects in the history of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ gleaming monuments to himself from the most improbable of building sites . <h> Advertisement <p> So Gaza , the bomb and corpse-strewn rubble field on the Mediterranean will become " The Riviera of the Middle East " . The icy wastes of Greenland are " an incredible place " , ideal for the construction of US military facilities and the development of mineral and fuel potential . As he threatened tariffs on his northern neighbour this week , he described the border between Canada and the US , fought over in war , settled by treaty and recognised in international law for two centuries , as an " artificial line " , the way a prospective property buyer might haggle with the local authority about the scope for access . <p> A second factor is the " Everything Everywhere All At Once " style of governing . Trump 's shock and awe @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with presidential initiatives , was well described by his former aide Steve Bannon in 2017 : if you keep doing a million new things at the same time , your opponents and the media ( the same thing , in their view ) wo n't have the capacity to scrutinise and oppose them effectively . <p> This applies especially when you propose some of the wilder stuff : the attention goes there and your other , radical but maybe not-completely-crazy ideas have space to get done . <p> So just as we were digesting the plan to shut down the US Agency for International Development , we 're going to talk about taking control of Gaza . @@120932260 <p> US involvement in Vietnam began on 8 March 1965 , when 3,500 marines were put ashore at Da Nang , South Vietnam . It effectively ended on 30 April 1975 with helicopter flights taking staff and dependants from the roof of the US Embassy in Saigon , although the war had long been lost by then . It is estimated that as many as 3 million people were killed in the conflict , including more than 58,000 members of the US armed forces and 2 million Vietnamese civilians . <p> Ad <p> The war that was supposed to defeat communism in southeast Asia scarred America 's psyche and powered the counter-cultural protest movement in the 1960s . It would also lead to a flurry of viscerally powerful feature films , most notably Apocalypse Now , Full Metal Jacket and The Deer Hunter . <p> Like those films , the six-part Apple TV+ documentary Vietnam : The War That Changed America has an evocative period soundtrack featuring Tamla Motown artists and rock bands like the Doors and the Animals . But the series , narrated by actor Ethan Hawke , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> " There have been a lot of fantastic series that tell you a lot about the politics and the terrible things that happened , " explains its director , Rob Coldstream , " but we wanted to put a different lens on the whole conflict . " <p> The Vietnam War , fought by the US against the North Vietnamese NVA and Viet Cong guerrillas , was the first to be broadcast on the evening news ; wherever the soldiers went , camera crews and reporters followed . " From a film-making point of view , it was absolutely magnificent , " says Coldstream . " We found hundreds of hours of footage , incredible combat scenes , soldiers almost being interviewed during the battle . " <p> Archival photo of troops arriving in Vietnam featured in Vietnam : The War That Changed America . Apple TV+ <p> Where possible , the producers have interviewed the people in that footage , an endeavour that required huge amounts of research but paid rich dividends . The men and women we meet are pensioners now and , like America itself @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ US veteran , CW Bowman , a " tunnel rat " tasked with searching the Viet Cong underground chambers , talks about the moment he killed a guerrilla with a machete and the disturbing feeling of power it gave him . " It was spine-tingling , " says Coldstream . " We were all crying in the room , this tough old dude opening up in that very vulnerable way . " <p> Life and death in Vietnam were often decided by the behaviour of those next to you , and throughout the series the film-makers reunite comrades who served together . Grey-haired and carrying extra pounds , their meetings in bars or coffee shops , where they blink back tears and embrace , are quietly poignant . <p> " It was the stories of the love or the friendships in different forms that are at the heart of the series , " says Coldstream . ' <p> The term " ethnic cleansing " originated during the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s and is a translation of " etnicko ciscenje " , which is Serbo-Croatian . Broadly speaking , it means the forcible removal of a distinct group of people from an area to which they belong to make the area ethnically homogenous . <p> The United Nations Commission of Experts investigated violations of international humanitarian law in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cleansing as " ... rendering an area ethnically homogeneous by using force or intimidation to remove persons of given groups from the area " . <p> A Palestinian youth surveys the rubble of Gaza City in November 2023 ( AFP ) <p> The following year , the commission called it " ... a purposeful policy designed by one ethnic or religious group to remove by violent and terror-inspiring means the civilian population of another ethnic or religious group from certain geographic areas " . <p> Ethnic cleansing , the commission said , can be implemented through serious international crimes , such as genocide , war crimes and crimes against humanity . <h> Does the term ' ethnic cleansing ' have legal status ? <p> Ethnic cleansing does not have an official legal definition and is not recognised as a crime . During Israel 's war on Gaza , the term has been used as a catch-all expression to describe both the war crimes and crimes against humanity relating to displacement , deportation and the forcible transfer of a civilian population . <p> The deportation or forcible transfer of a civilian @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ And if it is part of a widespread or systematic attack against civilians , then it 's also a crime against humanity , according to the Rome Statute that underpins the ICC . <p> Ardi Imseis is a professor of international law at Queen 's University and author of The UN and the Question of Palestine . He told MEE : " Under international humanitarian law and international criminal law , individual or mass forcible transfers , as well as deportations of protected persons from occupied territory to the territory of the occupying power or to that of any other country , occupied or not , are prohibited , regardless of their motive . " <p> The thinking behind the prohibition , Imseis said , was to stop any occupier usurping and colonising occupied territory , as Nazi Germany did during World War Two . <h> Are there examples of ethnic cleansing ? <p> The idea first emerged during the 1992-1995 Bosnian War , when Serb-led forces conducted ethnic cleansing against Bosniaks and Croats , not least during the Srebrenica genocide of July 1995 , when 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ men and boys uncovered in a mass grave near the eastern Bosnian village of Nova Kasaba , on 24 July 1996 ( Reuters ) <p> It has also been used retrospectively to describe the systemic campaigns of forced deportations and mass destruction that Nazi Germany carried out against Jews , Roma , Slavs , and other groups deemed " undesirable " in occupied Europe . <h> Has Israel been accused of ethnic cleansing before ? <p> For Palestinians , ethnic cleansing has echoes of the Nakba ( Arabic for catastrophe ) , when 750,000 people were forced from their homes and into neighbouring countries during the creation of Israel in 1948 . <p> The term has also been used to describe plans by Israeli settlers and far-right officials to forcibly displace Palestinians from Gaza and replace them with Israeli settlers . <p> Rights groups and activists say the expansion of settlements and displacement of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem is also part of the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians from Israeli-occupied lands . <h> Is Trump 's plan ethnic cleansing ? <p> Experts suggest Trump 's idea @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . @@120960946 <h> LATEST EDITORIAL <h> The African genocide on the Middle Passage <h> ROGER McKENZIE reflects on the enslavement , endurance and rebellion of Africans trafficked across the Atlantic and the untold sufferings of unknown ancestors <p> BRUTAL : Slaves above and below deck aboard the Albanoz , a captured Spanish slave ship in 1846 , so the people shown had in fact been liberated though not yet landed and released . Photo : National Maritime Museum/Creative Commons <p> ? <h> This is the last article you can read this month <h> You can read more article this month <h> You can read more articles this month <h> Sorry your limit is up for this month <p> THE recent memorials to the atrocities committed by Nazi Germany as well as the way the Palestinians of Gaza have resisted attempts to wipe them out has made me think about the centuries-old attempts to eliminate Africans . <p> No ! I do not think this is exaggerating what has happened to people of African descent during centuries of humiliation and exploitation . What happened was mass murder , torture on a mega-industrial scale @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ grateful for what we have . <p> Significant among the genocidal attacks on Africans was , of the course , the transatlantic slave trade which ran from the 15th to the 19th century . <p> Africans have never just stood by and allowed themselves to be murdered . There are countless examples of Africans , even after passing through the so-called " gates of no return " at the slave forts , fighting back against their captures . <p> In fact many historians now believe that there were active rebellions on these ships in around 10 per cent of the roughly 36,000 shipments of enslaved Africans across the notorious Middle Passage . <p> In one , in 1742 , the Jolly Batchelor was attacked by enslaved Africans while it was at dock in what became known as the Sierra Leone River . <p> The crew were killed during the fighting and the victorious Africans freed themselves and the people who were being held captive in the hold of the ship . <p> In another in 1752 , the Bristol-based ship , The Marlborough , was taken over by enslaved Africans @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the crew were killed and those who survived were forced to sail the ship back to Africa from where the enslaved Africans were freed . <p> One of the most famous rebellions recorded was on board The Amistad in 1839 . The ship was carrying enslaved Africans to a Spanish-owned plantation on Cuba . A group of Africans managed to escape from their chains and took control of the ship , killing several of the crew in the process . <p> The Africans were eventually recaptured and a court hearing was called to decide their fate . In a landmark ruling , the US Supreme Court granted the enslaved Africans their freedom . <p> This makes me enormously proud . I have no way of knowing the truth but I like to picture my ancestors being part of any uprisings on the ships they were forced onto . <p> Historians have estimated that something in excess of two million Africans died during the Middle Passage . Probably an underestimate . <p> Many died due to cramped conditions , which allowed diseases like measles and smallpox to quickly spread . Unsanitary @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , diarrhoea and dehydration . Many also arrived at their destination covered in sores and suffering from fever . <p> Africans were placed below deck , with males and females separated . Men and boys were placed toward the front and women and girls toward the back . <p> During the voyage across the Middle Passage , Africans were usually fed only once or twice a day . Some refused to eat , as a form of protest against their abduction . If they refused , they were often force-fed by their captors . <p> But many Africans also chose to throw themselves into the sea when the chance presented itself -- favouring death to enslavement . <p> Sharks are said to have regularly followed slave ships so that they could feast on Africans who were thrown overboard or who chose death over captivity . <p> These deaths are why I often refer to the Atlantic Ocean as a sacred burial ground . <p> The Middle Passage usually took more than seven weeks , with the length of the voyage depending on weather conditions in the Atlantic Ocean . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Africans escaped from their captors . They formed " Maroon Colonies " in remote regions of the colonial empires . <p> For those forced onto plantations life expectancy was around five years . They simply worked the Africans to death and replaced them with a new batch as they died out . <p> Rebellion also continued on the plantations . Among them was the Sam Sharp Rebellion , otherwise known as the Great Jamaican Slave Revolt of 1831-32 . This was an 11-day uprising by around 60,000 enslaved Africans . <p> The uprising was led by an African Baptist deacon , Sam Sharp . Although the uprising was brutally suppressed by the British , it is widely recognised as having played a major role in the eventual abolition of slavery throughout the British empire in 1834 . <p> We were never meant to survive enslavement -- at least not intact . Many of us did not but the fact that I am able to sit here and tap out my ramblings on a laptop is testament to the strength of my ancestors who went before me . <p> Without them @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ here today and do not enjoy the luxury of giving up the fight . <p> The ancestors endured chains , the whip and humiliations on a daily basis . For that I thank them and praise their spirit of resistance . I assure them that their spirit of survival and resistance remains in many of us today .

@@120967349 <p> The US President 's brand of diplomacy is built on taking radical positions <p> February 6 , 2025 10:31 <p> Trump 's extreme approach to diplomacy could give the US more leverage over the future of the Middle East ( Image : Getty ) <p> 2 min read <p> For decades , US policy on the Israeli-Arab/Palestinian conflict has hinged on detailed peace plans built on conventional diplomacy . Not so with Donald Trump . His approach is transactional , prioritising leverage over meticulous blueprints . The Abraham Accords were not the result of a grand strategy but rather a series of ad hoc trade-offs : Netanyahu shelved annexation in exchange for UAE normalisation ; Morocco gained US recognition of Western Sahara in return for ties with Israel . These precedents are key to understanding Trump 's latest vision for Gaza . <p> Trump has three stated objectives related to Gaza : a ceasefire and the return of all hostages , the extension of the Abraham Accords to include Saudi Arabia , and the rebuilding of Gaza under American supervision -- including the relocation of Gaza 's population during @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is a ceasefire and hostage return . By publicly floating a relocation plan , Trump increases his bargaining power over both Israel and Hamas . For Netanyahu , Trump 's support has helped shore up his position -- not only with the Israeli public but , crucially , with his far-right coalition partners . Dangling his Gaza plan in front of figures like Bezalel Smotrich makes it easier for them to accept a ceasefire as a necessary step toward larger strategic gains . <p> Simultaneously , Trump exerts pressure on Hamas . Israel demands that Hamas ' leadership go into exile and that the group disarm . If Hamas refuses , it risks US backing for an Israeli military campaign to impose those terms . Furthermore , with Hezbollah and Iran weakened , Hamas ' previous strategy -- provoking a regional war -- looks far less viable than it did a year ago . <p> However , the majority of Gazans will not voluntarily opt to leave . While some third countries might accept limited numbers , Arab states reject mass relocation outright . Even Netanyahu 's government , with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Doing so could set the West Bank ablaze , unravel Israel 's normalisation and peace agreements , and destabilise pro-Western regimes -- gifting Iran , ISIS , and similar groups a massive political boost . <p> Assuming Israel dismantles Hamas ' governing capability power within a timeframe acceptable to Trump -- a major " if " -- Gaza will be left in a political vacuum . Trump has signalled that he does not want Israeli occupation or settler return , raising the question of who will fill the void . At this point , America 's Arab allies might seek to head off Trump 's relocation plan by investing heavily in Gaza 's reconstruction , with most of its population remaining . In return , Trump could leverage his support for Netanyahu to extract the concessions needed to secure Saudi normalisation -- potentially an " over-the-horizon " Palestinian state , conditional on reforming the Palestinian Authority . <p> This scenario , however , is vulnerable to multiple points of failure -- not least Trump himself . He is instinctively isolationist , having threatened to leave NATO , pushed for withdrawal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ all of America 's 25,000 troops from South Korea in exchange for a nuclear deal with North Korea . How likely is it that he would take on a massive commitment in Gaza -- a potential quagmire where American forces would be constantly targeted by radical Islamist militias ? <p> Trump 's brand of diplomacy is built on pushing extremes to shift negotiations in his favour . By introducing a radical alternative -- relocation -- he forces regional players to make concessions to prevent it from materialising . But there is a difference between entertaining the idea of population transfer in principle and making it an actionable priority . For Trump , relocation is a tool , not a strategic goal . <p> Professor Jonathan Rynhold is the head of the Political Studies department at Bar-Ilan University and a senior researcher at the Begin-Sadat Centre for Strategic Studies .

@@121016894 <h> Times letters : Surrendering the Chagos Islands to Mauritius <p> Sir , I am perplexed by suggestions that the UK may be under some obligation under international law to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius . First , as even the Foreign Office recognises , the opinion of the International Court of Justice ( ICJ ) was purely advisory , not binding . Second , it was based on a UN General Assembly resolution . Such resolutions are not legally binding . Third , when the UK signed up to the ICJ our declaration specifically said that the government of the UK " accepts ... the jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice ... other than ... any dispute with the government of any country which is or has been a member of the Commonwealth " , as is Mauritius . Hence any opinion of the ICJ would be triply non-binding . Ministers never mention these facts . Either they are unaware of them or they do not want us to know.Lord LilleyFormer deputy leader of the Conservative Party ; London SW1 <p> Sir , As you point @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Feb 6 ) , it was the Tories who started negotiations with Mauritius in 2019 after a hostile International Court of Justice opinion , an error of judgment that has been compounded by the present administration . Think of the midnight raids on immigrant neighbourhoods , the children torn from schools , the deportation camps . <p> But the policies which will impact most on the UK and Europe are likely to be around tariffs , Ukraine , Nato and the Middle East . <p> Tariffs are Trump 's preferred instrument of coercion and were always bound to be deployed early on . He initially imposed 25 per cent tariffs on imports from Canada and Mexico -- and a 10 per cent rise in current tariffs on China -- although he has since agreed to hold off imposing the tariffs on Mexico and Canada after both countries agreed to strengthen their respective US border security . <p> Next , Trump will take action against the EU because " they treat us very unfairly " . This is already prompting retaliatory tariffs , threatening a trade war which damages everyone @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ global economic growth , job losses , higher inflation and disrupted supply chains , but Trump appears immovable . <p> Can the UK avoid this tariff carnage ? Well , maybe . Trump has said " the UK is out of line " but " Starmer has been very nice " and something " can be worked out " . Unlike Germany , with its huge surplus , our trade is in rough balance with the US and we buy billions of dollars of US military equipment , from F-35s to Apache helicopters . So , damage the UK economy and there 'll be less money to spend on defence . <p> Even if the UK manages to escape tariffs , trade wars with others will hurt our economy significantly . The threat of US tariffs will hang over us for the next four years . When Trump says " we can work something out " , he means there will be a price to pay ; perhaps the UK opening its markets to US agricultural exports -- a disaster-in-waiting for British farmers . <p> On Ukraine , Trump has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . He must think that Russia is now winning this war , albeit at the huge cost of 1,200 casualties a day . It is hard to see Volodymyr Zelensky accepting a deal that gives territory over to Russia and stops them from joining Nato . If a ceasefire is within grasp , Trump will expect Europe , not the US , to provide any security guarantees needed to get Ukraine over the line . Regardless , all scenarios look exceptionally difficult for the Europeans . <p> As for Nato , Trump has bitterly criticised Nato allies for falling short of their commitments on defence spending . Trump can take a victory lap in the first Nato summit of his second term : 23 of Nato 's 32 members are now at two per cent of GDP . But to think that this is problem solved is to misread Trump . But to now suggest that Gazans should be forced to leave the territory is seriously destabilising and risks more extremism and conflict . <p> The certainties of the postwar decades have gone . He had a history of refusing to take medication at home . <p> This raises an important @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it is the belief that somebody with a psychotic illness severe enough to get them sectioned -- compelled to stay in a psychiatric hospital under the Mental Health Act -- somehow retains enough rationality to take crucial decisions about their medication . It seems to me obvious that they no longer possess that power of judgement , and that , sadly , is what severe mental illness is all about . Often , patients are unaware that they are mentally ill , so they see their medication as persecution . <p> It is surely absurd to assume that a person who has essentially lost their reason still retains sufficient good enough judgement to make decisions affecting themselves . As one psychiatrist pointed out to me : " Studies show that even a mild depression impairs people 's ability to take sensible decisions , so imagine what a full-blown psychosis does . " <p> Yet many psychiatrists , who should know better , will not force a desperately ill patient to take necessary medication -- though that is the only way that they can regain their sanity . Compulsion does not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . The most effective drug for people suffering from paranoid schizophrenia is usually clozapine , which is not given as a depot injection because of possible negative side effects . <p> Patients may covertly conceal pills in their mouth and not swallow them , so the best way of ensuring that they do so is for the clozapine to be given to them in dilute form in a glass of water and a nurse to stay nearby for half an hour to make sure that they do not deliberately sick up the medication . Had this been done in the case of Calocane , the three people he killed at random would most likely still be alive today . <h> Beneath the Radar <p> Donald Trump and Elon Musk have attacked USAID as " an atrocity " and partially closed it down , but there is no doubt that it has saved millions of lives and improved the lives of millions more . <p> Aid agencies are seldom popular in any donor country because people feel that they are giving away money , which could be better spent at home @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is often being distributed in failed or failing states , it is always possible to find evidence of malfeasance . <p> About 10 years ago in Afghanistan , I employed an Afghan as a translator and guide whose previous job was with USAID . He said he had left them as his work had got too dangerous because he was employed to monitor the progress of projects outside Kabul , which USAID was funding . It was considered too dangerous for American citizens working for the agency to visit personally the project sites . Instead , they followed their progress through videos and photographs sent electronically by recipients of the aid . <p> The Afghan working for me had gone to Kandahar to look at some USAID-funded schemes and had made an interesting discovery : often the projects did not exist . What did exist was a sort of film studio which , for a stiff fee , would make convincing videos of some scheme -- say a vegetable-packing plant -- in operation with its workers busily sorting carrots or cauliflowers for market . <p> On another occasion , he @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to the owners and drew their attention to the absence of chickens . They gave him a steady look and remarked that this might be so , but he should remember that " it is a long road back to Kabul " . In other words , they would kill him on the road , if he denounced them to USAID . In the event , he did go back to Kabul -- and resigned his job immediately . <p> I am a little ambivalent about telling this story because it seems to confirm all the horror stories told by the anti-aid lobby . On the contrary , most of my encounters with aid agencies showed them to be heroic and essential providers to people who have nothing . I still have a picture in my mind of two relaxed UN workers , originally from Turkey and Finland , standing in the snow in Iraqi Kurdistan in 1991 , who explained to me how they planned to house several hundred thousand Kurdish refugees before winter set in . They knew exactly down to the last nail and ton of concrete @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ mountain roads . Without in any way dismissing the trauma of that day for Israelis , we can see how this trauma was intensified by the relentless coverage on Israeli media , which amplified the sense of fear and reinforced a shocking indifference to the genocide being waged less than 80km from Tel Aviv . <p> Author Naomi Klein has referred to this as the " weaponisation of trauma " . She argues that the state of shock from 7 October is maintained so that there can never be recovery , keeping people in a state of raw emotion that precludes any possibility for empathy , thoughtful analysis , or any guilt or shame @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> The obverse of this hyper-emotionality is the refusal to accept that Palestinians are entitled to any emotional display and to label any such displays as a threat . The " banning of joy " fits with a pattern of surveillance over not only the movements , activities and speech of Palestinians but also their emotions . <p> The policing of emotions is another aspect of the deep intrusion of the settler-colonial state into the subjective and intimate worlds of the subject people . For example , Palestinians who are held up for hours at a checkpoint and express their frustration by shouting or hooting their car horns are liable to be punished . As a result , feelings of rage and fury have to be suppressed . <h> Bargaining chip <p> Public displays of emotion , whether joy at the release of prisoners or grief at the burial of martyrs , are policed in multiple ways . @@121050475 <h> Step forward Sir Keir Starmer - the wrong man at the wrong time <p> Keir Starmer has proven himself not to be the man to walk the current political tightrope ( Image : Derek McArthur ) <p> For all my carping over Sir Keir Starmer , I do n't envy him . A technocrat in an age of populism , he has come to power at the worst possible time . Having inherited an economy trashed by successive Tory governments , he is caught between a talus of rocks and a sierra of hard places . <p> Stuck with a Brexit he actively opposed ( but can not overturn ) , and a US president he must abhor ( but can not disown ) , he now faces a third existential threat : a rapidly rising Reform UK with its eyes firmly fixed on his red-wall voters , and much of the right-wing media in its thrall . <p> On the one hand , Starmer wants to rekindle the UK 's tattered relationship with the EU , on the other he wants to head off Donald Trump 's threatened @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ yet increasingly fractured relationship with the US . But he ca n't cosy up to Europe without poking the Reform bear , and attracting negative headlines from the Daily Mail ; and he ca n't cosy up to Trump without aggravating the left and morally compromising himself . <p> So far , he has walked the political tightrope in a way his advocates might describe as deft and his critics as cynical . He has courted the EU - gaining applause from EU leaders - without committing to any specific vision of the future , or outlining concessions he might be willing to make . <p> This week he found a ( weasel ) way to express his disapproval of Trump 's positioning of Gaza as a real estate opportunity without condemning the man himself ( or using tough words like " genocide " or " ethnic cleansing " ) . But with Reform 's popularity waxing as Starmer 's approval ratings wane ; with the EU beset by both Russia and the US , and Trump 's behaviour degenerating with each executive order , the rope is fast fraying @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The Prime Minister 's caution is both his greatest asset and his greatest liability . In an era dominated by political shock-jocks , a degree of caginess is welcome . But there comes a point where hedging one 's bets tips from canny pragmatism into an abdication of responsibility . <p> Moreover , most people have no respect for the kind of shapeshifting we witnessed in Peter Mandelson 's conversion from Trump despiser to Trump admirer . " Say what you like about Nigel Farage , " the demographic being hit on by Reform will opine as they sup their pints at Wetherspoons up and down the country , " but at least you know where he stands " . <p> The time for Starmer to decide where he stands is nigh . The EU leaders who have signed up to his May summit have made it clear they expect it to produce concrete results . If that is to happen , he will have to come up with a concrete position : on defence , fishing rights , and cooperation on energy and climate policies . <p> It wo @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ over a youth mobility scheme , which the EU is adamant it wants , and which would be a huge boost for young people , but which Home Secretary Yvette Cooper has already ruled because it would increase net migration . <p> The very word " migration " is a trigger for those within the party whose constituencies are vulnerable to Reform advances and who are urging Starmer to talk even tougher on the small boats and traffickers . But - short of going full-fat fascism - it 's impossible to outflank Reform on xenophobia . <p> Keir Starmer with hard-right Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni ( Image : free ) Sure , the Prime Minister can scurry off to Italy for chats with Giorgia Meloni , and promise to treat smugglers like terrorists . But no one on the right is ever going to believe he hates asylum seekers more than Farage . And most of us on the left do n't want to hear him pretend that he does . <p> The significance of the UK 's relationship with the US can not be underestimated in terms of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the EU looks like the better bet . Putin 's expansionist ambitions make European solidarity more urgent than ever , while the UK is still heavily reliant on the EU for trade . A new security deal makes sense , especially given Trump 's ambivalence on NATO . Meanwhile , the US president 's smash and grab attitude towards Canada and Greenland shows he is not to be trusted . <p> Even if Starmer 's overtures lead to the UK avoiding tariffs , who is to say that position would be sustained ? If the experiences of Canada and Mexico are anything to go by , Trump intends to use those tariffs to beat other countries into submission . Their shadow will continue to loom . At least any treaty thrashed out with the EU is likely to be honoured . <p> Nor does it seem likely Trump is going to become any more measured over time . It 's taken less than three weeks for most European countries to move from tones of reluctant diplomacy to borderline contempt as he continues to up the ante . Even the impartiality-obsessed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Starmer 's words on Gaza seemed muted compared to many other world leaders and statesmen . <p> " This would be a serious violation of international law and an obstacle to a two state solution , " said French Foreign Ministry spokesman , Christophe Lemoine . Brazil 's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said : " This is something incomprehensible to any human being . " <p> Will Starmer be more explicit the next time Trump proposes something that flies in the face of all that is decent ? Or the time after that ? Because at some point his more passive approach is going to become untenable . <p> As for Reform , it would be a mistake to see it as Trumpism-lite . There are distinct differences between the two movements and many Reform supporters are not fans of MAGA or the US president . Farage was quick to criticise Elon Musk over his support for Tommy Robinson , which could indicate he feels secure enough to be able to dispense friendly criticism or that he is confident his party is operating on entirely its own terms @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ does a support for Reform necessarily translate into a preference for trans-Atlantic intimacy . A YouGov poll out this week showed only 11% of people judged Brexit to be a success with one in six Leave voters believing the country made a mistake . More than two thirds of the population ( including 60% of Leave voters and 53% of Reform voters ) would favour a closer relationship with the EU without formally joining any part of it while 55% would support a complete undoing of Brexit . So while Starmer must be mindful of the Reform threat he should not be allowing it to shape his policies . <p> This is even more true in Scotland where recent polls suggest there is nothing the SNP can do to get itself thrown out of power , and Labour 's general election resurgence looks set to be short-lived . @@121050931 <h> Mark Brown : The roles played by Scots in the emergence of America 's far-right <h> The roles played by Scots in the emergence of America 's far-right <p> We in Scotland should remember the roles played by Scots , both for and against , the emergence of America 's far-right <p> TAKE a walk in the Dean Cemetery on the west side of Edinburgh and you will find a memorial that is emblazoned with the distinctive battle flag of the Confederacy during the US Civil War of 1861-65 . <p> The monument is dedicated to Edinburgh-born Robert A Smith , who served as a colonel in the Confederate Army . <p> A quiet burial ground in Scotland 's capital city might seem a world away from the chaos and cruelty of the opening weeks of the second presidential term of Donald Trump , but there is a very real sense in which Smith , and thousands of other Scottish Confederates , are connected to the incumbent of the White House . <p> Trump 's presidency has begun -- as many people feared it would -- with a flurry @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ out as unambiguously of the far-right . <p> ( Image : Christopher Furlong , Getty Images ) <p> At Trump 's victory rally , Elon Musk ( who is a supporter of both the multiply convicted English fascist Tommy Robinson and the far-right AfD/Alternative for Germany ) threw two Nazi salutes . The new president has promised the " biggest deportation programme " in US history . <p> He also ordered blanket pardons for what he ludicrously calls " the January 6 hostages " , releasing almost 1600 criminals who were convicted for their roles in the far-right insurrection at the Capitol in January 2021 . These include the former leader of the fascist Proud Boys movement Enrique Tarrio , who was serving a 22-year term for orchestrating the deadly assault on the Capitol building . <p> Trump 's foreign policy -- particularly his proposal to ethnically cleanse Gaza of its 2.1 million Palestinian people , transferring control of the strip to Washington -- looks like American imperialism on steroids . <p> It is hardly surprising , therefore , that many commentators have been seeking historical parallels with which to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ no doubt , by Musk 's sieg heiling at the Washington rally -- have drawn comparisons with the Nazi regime that came to power in Germany in 1933 . <p> However -- tempting as it might be for admirers of American democracy to see Trumpism as the importation of an alien , European ideology into the political system of the United States -- the fact is that the 47th president stands in a homegrown far-right tradition that has a long and deplorable history . It 's a tradition , indeed , in which -- like so many aspects of American life -- Scots have played a notable and prominent role . <p> The Confederacy of 11 southern states -- a breakaway republic begun in 1860 -- was dedicated to the preservation of the system of slavery of African people in North America . Thousands of Scots served in the Confederate Army as soldiers and medics . <p> There are no accurate records as to their exact numbers , but it is believed to be some way short of the estimated 50,000 Scots who served in Abraham Lincoln 's Union Army @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ s in the Confederate war effort , and the subsequent racial politics of the US , should not be underestimated . <p> Take America 's most notorious , murderous white supremacist organisation -- the Ku Klux Klan ( KKK ) -- for example . The Klan has its origins in a group formed in 1865 , in the immediate aftermath of the Civil War , by six former Confederate officers of Scottish and Irish descent . <p> The words " Ku Klux " are widely believed to be a reference to the Greek word kyklos ( meaning circle or ring ) , with the word " Klan " being added to emphasise the Scottishness or Celticness of the organisation . From the Confederate Army to the KKK , the involvement of Scots in the evolution of racist and far-right politics in the US marks the dark side of Scottish influence in American history . <p> Take the aforementioned Colonel Smith , for example . This Scottish Confederate died , aged 26 , from wounds sustained at the Battle of Munfordville , Kentucky in 1862 . So well regarded was he @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ time , as a bodyguard to Jefferson Davis , the president of the Confederacy . <p> The memorial to Smith in Edinburgh is not the only one . <p> In Hart County , Kentucky , there stands a monument -- a 25-foot high , limestone obelisk -- that was erected by Smith 's brother , the wealthy Scottish businessman James Smith , in 1884 . The inscription on it is dedicated to : " The sacrifice of Col. Robt . A Smith and his regiment the 10th Mississippi . " <p> A further inscription refers to the widely believed theory that the deaths of Smith and many of his men were caused by an unscrupulous order from Brigadier General James R Chalmers . The brigadier is believed to have feared that Smith -- a rising star of the Confederate Army -- was a threat to his position . <p> Consequently , the theory goes , Chalmers broke with army protocol and -- without consultation with his superior officers -- ordered that Smith lead an immediate , and premature , attack on Union forces . After questioning the military sense of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ believed to have said ( as is inscribed on the Kentucky monument ) : " The duty is mine , but the responsibility lies elsewhere . " <p> This tale of treachery and fatal obedience has only served to solidify Smith 's place in Confederate folklore . <p> Another famous Scottish Confederate is Edinburgh-born Kate Cumming . Having migrated from Scotland with her family as a child and settled in Alabama , Cumming volunteered as a nurse in the new Confederate hospital system following her brother 's decision to enlist in the Confederate Army . <p> Cumming served as a matron in Confederate hospitals throughout the Civil War . Her fame -- or infamy ( according to taste ) -- was secured in large part by her authorship of the book A Journal Of Hospital Life In The Confederate Army Of Tennessee From The Battle Of Shiloh To The End Of The War . <p> Cumming 's book -- which is one of very few accounts of nursing in the Confederacy during the war -- shows her to be an unrepentant and dedicated supporter of the Confederate cause . As @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that the white population of the slave-owning South -- rather than the African slaves themselves -- were the real victims in 19th-century America . <p> Writing in the aftermath of the war , she refers to the states of the renegade Southern republic as a nation distinct from Lincoln 's Union . In the introduction to the journal , she writes : " The southerner may learn a lesson from the superhuman endurance of the glorious dead and mutilated living who so nobly did their duty in their country 's hour of peril . <p> " And the northerner , I trust , when he has brought in review before him the wrongs of every kind inflicted on us , will cry , Enough ! they have suffered enough ... " <p> On the subject of southern war crimes -- for which former Confederate military figures were then being tried -- Cumming is unapologetic : " We starved their prisoners ! Back in Scotland -- which had been home to so many slave owners and other slavery profiteers ( such as tobacco merchants ) -- the abolition of slavery in 1833 did not deter Clydeside 's shipbuilders from making their fortunes supplying boats to the Confederacy . <p> The Union forces operated a sea blockade of the southern Atlantic coast in an effort to starve the Confederacy of weapons and other supplies . The shipyards on the Clyde provided the South with dozens of fast shallow steamers -- known as " blockade runners " -- @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Clyde-built ships supplied southern ports such as Wilmington and Charleston with weapons and various other goods . On their return journeys , they brought out cargoes of slave cotton , the profits of which were used to finance the Confederate war effort . <p> These blockade-running ships -- which were often crewed by Scots -- played a crucial role , not only for the Confederate military and the Southern economy , but also for the economy of the British state . The profits for the Clyde shipbuilders and blockade-runners were considerable . <p> As , often , were the Confederate sympathies of many of those Scottish businessmen . " <p> Indeed , if we consider the classic definition of Dutch political scientist Cas Mudde , we see that it applies perfectly to the Saiedian vision . Mudde defines populism as " a thin-centred ideology that considers society to be ultimately separated into two homogenous and antagonistic groups : ' the pure people ' and ' the corrupt elite @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of the volonte generale general will of the people " . <p> This vision is reflected in Saied 's 2019 campaign slogan " the people want " . <p> It is important to emphasise that when Saied speaks of the people , he does not mean a majority of citizens or a mass whose critical size can represent the Tunisian population . Saied 's people are those who think like him and support him unconditionally - even if they are a minority . <p> During the online consultation organised in 2022 , Tunisians had to choose three reforms deemed priorities among five proposals . The adoption of a new constitution received only 36 percent of the votes , against 38 percent in favour of a partial revision of the fundamental law . <p> However , it was the minority choice that was picked by Saied and the country was given a new fundamental law . <p> Let us also recall that this consultation , supposed to represent the popular will , only gathered 534,915 participants - barely 5 percent of the electorate - knowing that it was open to segments @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ forces , minors aged 16 to 18 ) . <p> The same applies to the constitutional referendum of 25 July 2022 . If the Soviet-style score obtained by the " yes " ( 94.5 percent ) can seem impressive , it goes down to 28.5 percent when related to the electorate . <h> Bringing justice into line <p> On 25 July 2021 , by listing the " exceptional measures " he had just adopted ( freezing parliamentary activities , lifting MPs ' immunity and dismissing Prime Minister Hichem Mechichi ) , Saied announced his intention to head the public prosecutor 's department . Although this provision was not directly implemented , a methodical undertaking to bring justice into line started . <p> Under the guise of cleaning up the judicial corps , the regime annihilated all guarantees of the judiciary 's independence . <p> By relegating the judiciary ' power ' to the rank of a simple ' function ' , Saied controlled a machine capable of crushing his opponents and creating a climate of terror in society <p> By relegating the judiciary " power " to the rank of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ capable of crushing his opponents and creating a climate of terror in society . In this chapter , we will study the different phases of this process of subjugating the most important counter-power that can exist in a democratic society . <p> The bringing of justice into line is undoubtedly the most significant regression since 25 July 2021 . Judges are now subject to a double submission . The most obvious is that of an executive who no longer even tries to pretend to respect the independence of justice . <p> But magistrates are also under the heel of the security forces , who have the ear of the authorities and are capable of breaking the career of any judge . <p> It should be noted that resistance to this movement is very weak . The Judges ' Union , the most representative body , welcomed the latest transfer movement . ( In September 2023 , Saied 's justice minister transferred magistrates whose rulings are deemed not compliant with the president 's will , although according to the constitution , they can not be relocated against their will . ) @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ranks of magistrates , repressive policies and the abusive use of custodial sentences are in the DNA of a profession that needs a profound revolution in terms of both training and legislative texts . <h> The permanent conspiracy <p> What does the naming of Storm Daniel , artificial intelligence and the shortage of raw materials have in common ? <p> They are all , in Saied 's rhetoric , the result of conspiracies . If conspiracy theories are used by many rulers around the world , under Saied , it is a real governing mode . <p> By multiplying conspiracy theories , the ruler offers a reassuring speech which is quite capable of legitimising the government in power . <p> ( These theories ) maintain the idea of ? ? a generalised conspiracy against Tunisians .
